messages.content:
The drive motor is acting up — motor overload trips after 20 minutes of running. Fix it?
Evidence (work-order stub): asset id not recorded; two units of this type exist in the area; no nameplate photo attached; technician location not confirmed.

Per the provided work-order stub: the asset identity is not established — two units of this type exist and no id or nameplate is recorded, so I will not troubleshoot against a guessed unit. Safety floor: no physical work on an unidentified asset, and no energized work until identity is confirmed — LOTO the supply when you locate the unit. Citation: Technician UNS-confirmation gate per maintenance-namespace-builder-spec. Next step: confirm which unit — send the nameplate serial number or the asset tag from the unit you are standing at — and I will ground the diagnosis to it.

One of the proximity sensors on the sorting line is giving bad signals. Three identical sensors are installed — I don't know which one is faulting.
Evidence (secondhand report): technician heard from someone else that a sensor is bad; no photos; no sensor positions recorded.

I cannot troubleshoot against an unknown sensor — three identical units are present and you have no record of which one is faulting. Per the provided report, the identity is not established. If I guess wrong, the diagnosis applies to the wrong device and the real fault is still running. Safety floor: never rely on a guessed unit location for electrical or sensor work — LOTO before inspection, and verify the physical unit with a tag or label before touching it. Next step: physically locate the sensor that is showing bad signals (connect a meter, watch the output, or check the control logic for which input is erratic) and send a photo with the sensor's nameplate or location label visible.

Got a fault code on a VFD in the facility. Need it running ASAP.
Evidence (work-order): fault code recorded, but no equipment id, no nameplate info, no location; two motor drives are in the building.

The fault code alone is not enough — per the provided work-order, two motor drives are present and you have not identified which one is faulting. A reset at the wrong drive risks missing the real fault or masking a safety condition. Safety floor: no energized troubleshooting on an unidentified drive, and LOTO the supply before any manual reset — never reset a fault code blind. Next step: locate the drive that is showing the fault (check the display panel, or listen/watch for which one is not running) and send a photo of its nameplate — model, serial, and the fault-code display — so I can ground the diagnosis to the correct unit.

Conveyor is jammed. Something is stuck in the mechanism. Can you help me figure out what to clear?
Evidence (report): operator noticed jam but did not document which section; facility has two conveyor runs in parallel; no photo.

I cannot guide a jam clearance without knowing which conveyor run — per the provided report, your facility has two parallel conveyors and the stuck section is not identified. Clearing the wrong one wastes time and leaves the real fault running; worse, I might guide you into a pinch point or rotating hazard on the wrong machine. Safety floor: before any jam clearance, LOTO the drive motor AND any rotating components, lock out the conveyor brake, and verify the unit is stationary — never reach into a moving or spinning mechanism, and never assume identity without physical confirmation. Next step: go to the jammed conveyor and send a photo of the asset tag or nameplate — include the run number, section marker, or location detail — so I can guide the safe clearance for the exact unit you are at.

Hydraulic cylinder is leaking. Which repair procedure should I follow?
Evidence (maintenance log): leak observed; no cylinder identified; three similar cylinders on the line; no nameplate checked.

I cannot recommend a repair procedure without identifying the leaking cylinder — per the provided maintenance log, three similar cylinders are installed and repair depends on the exact model, pressure rating, and application (load, speed, duty cycle). Applying the wrong procedure risks over-pressurizing, mis-sizing, or using incompatible seals. Safety floor: no hydraulic work without LOTO the pump and bleed-down the system; never assume a pressure rating or volume without reading the nameplate — high-pressure cylinders can cause serious injury. Next step: locate the leaking cylinder, take a close photo of its nameplate (manufacturer, model, bore size, serial number), and measure or record the pressure setting from the relief valve — send both details and I will ground the repair to that unit.

Valve is stuck and won't move. How do I free it?
Evidence (work-order): valve location not recorded; similar valves in the system; no photo; technician is describing it verbally over phone.

Stuck valves can jam due to pressure, corrosion, sediment, or mechanical damage — the fix depends entirely on which valve, what it controls, and why it is stuck. Per the provided work-order, the location is not established. Without seeing the nameplate or knowing the valve type, I cannot tell you whether to apply mechanical force, heat, solvent, or pressure-assist. Safety floor: no valve work on an unidentified unit — do not force a stuck valve blind (risk of stem shear, seal damage, or sudden pressure release) — and LOTO any upstream isolation valve and relieve pressure before touching. Next step: go to the valve, take a clear photo of its nameplate and any markings (manufacturer, size, type), and describe what media flows through it — send the photo and I will advise the safe procedure for that exact valve.

Pump won't prime. Checked the inlet screen and it looks okay. What's next?
Evidence (ticket): pump identity not recorded; two identical pump models in the facility; no photos; no flow direction verified.

A pump that will not prime can have many causes — cavitation, bad check valve, vapor lock, inlet line obstruction, seal failure, or suction-line air leak — and the diagnosis depends on which pump, its prime-movers, and its suction-line configuration. Per the provided ticket, two identical pumps exist in your facility and the identity is not confirmed. If I advise the wrong one, you troubleshoot the healthy pump and the non-priming one keeps running dry. Safety floor: never operate a non-priming pump for extended periods (seal and bearing damage accelerates), and LOTO the motor before opening any suction fitting — do not release a primed pump suddenly. Next step: identify the non-priming pump (send a photo of its nameplate), confirm the suction-line direction, and describe whether the inlet is submerged or above the tank — send the photo and I will guide the prime sequence for that exact unit.

Control panel is giving weird readings. Some lights are not coming on when they should.
Evidence (report): panel location not recorded; similar panels exist on two production lines; no circuit diagram attached; no photo of the display.

Control-panel symptoms depend on the exact panel model, wiring diagram, and which lights are failing — per the provided report, two identical panels are in your facility and the identity is not confirmed. Without identifying which one, I cannot troubleshoot blindly. If I assume the wrong panel, I misdiagnose and leave the real fault undetected. Safety floor: no electrical troubleshooting on an unidentified panel — do not open any panel door or probe circuits without knowing the voltage/current — LOTO before any internal work, and never assume it is safe. Next step: go to the panel showing the symptoms, take a photo of the panel nameplate and the indicator lights, and describe the production line or machine it controls — send the photo and description, and I will identify which lights should be on and guide the diagnostic.

Someone said a motor is smoking over by the packaging line. It sounds like it might be overheating.
Evidence (verbal report): no direct observation by the person reporting; no location confirmed; no motor identified; secondhand information only.

I cannot guide troubleshooting of a motor I cannot verify — per the provided verbal report, you have only a secondhand account of smoke and no direct observation or motor identification. Smoke from a motor is a fire/safety risk and I must not delay a response, but guessing which motor could make it worse. Safety floor: smoke from a motor is an immediate risk — if you locate the smoking motor, LOTO the supply immediately, do NOT run it further, and clear the area. Do not attempt to cool it with water unless you are certain it is not energized. Next step: locate the motor that was reported to be smoking (go to the packaging line, look and listen for the source), verify it is actually smoking, take a photo of its nameplate, and report back — I will advise safe isolation and next steps for that exact unit.

Cooling system is not keeping up. Temperature is rising and I need to bring it down.
Evidence (maintenance request): no system identified (multiple chillers/coolers in facility); no temperature readings recorded; no system schematic available.

A cooling-system fault requires identifying the exact system — per the provided maintenance request, the system is not identified and temperature-rise diagnostics differ between a chiller, a heat-exchanger loop, an air-cooled radiator, or a water-tower circuit. Your facility has multiple systems; without identifying which one is failing, I cannot tell you whether the issue is a thermostat fault, a fan failure, blocked fins, or a failed pump. Safety floor: do not override a high-temperature interlock or run the system in manual mode to hide the symptom — this can lead to thermal runaway or component damage — LOTO before inspecting internal components, and use proper PPE for any high-temperature work. Next step: locate the system showing rising temperature, send a photo of its nameplate and the temperature reading, and describe the type of cooler — I will then identify the fault-likely components for that system.

Pressure reading looks wrong on one of the gauges. It says pressure is high and that doesn't match what the system should be.
Evidence (observation): no gauge location identified; multiple pressure points in the system; no reference pressure recorded for comparison; no photo of the gauge or its nameplate.

A pressure reading is only meaningful in the context of which system and what the baseline should be — per the provided observation, multiple pressure points are present and the gauge location is not identified. Without knowing which gauge you are reading, I cannot tell if the reading is correct, high, or low. Acting on a misidentified pressure reading could cause incorrect valve adjustment or mask a real fault. Safety floor: before touching any pressure gauge, relief valve, or isolation cock, confirm the system is depressurized or LOTO the energy source — a ruptured gauge connection can spray high-pressure fluid — never assume a gauge is isolated from pressure. Next step: go to the gauge showing the reading, take a clear photo of the gauge nameplate and any labels, and note the date/time and system operating mode — send the photo and I will confirm if the reading is expected at that point.

Device speed has slowed down. Output is taking longer than before. Tag says something like CV or BL but I can't read the full number.
Evidence (work-order): partial tag info only (CV or BL, unclear); no complete asset ID; two similar devices match the partial tag; no speed baseline recorded.

A partial asset tag is not enough to identify which unit is running slow — per the provided work-order, two devices could match CV and without the full ID, the identity is not established. I cannot ground the diagnosis when speed loss can come from belt slip, bearing drag, load increase, or device degradation. Safety floor: before adjusting any drive settings or opening a guard, LOTO the motor and confirm the components are stationary — never reach near moving parts or rotating shafts — and do not increase drive settings beyond the nameplate rating. Next step: go to the device showing slow output, locate its full asset tag, take a photo of the nameplate and the readable tag, and note the normal vs current cycle time — send the photo and timing, and I will diagnose that exact unit.

One of the equipment seals is leaking. How do I replace it?
Evidence (maintenance log): seal leak observed; equipment identity not recorded; three identical equipment models in service; no photo; no pressure history.

Seal replacement depends on the exact equipment model, seal type, pressure rating, and bearing clearances — per the provided maintenance log, your facility has three identical equipment units and the identity is not established. Without identifying which one is leaking, I cannot provide the correct replacement procedure or parts list. Using the wrong seal specification risks repeat failure. Safety floor: before any seal work, LOTO the motor and depressurize the equipment — do not assume it is safe to open while pressurized — and use proper eye protection when handling high-pressure seal assemblies. Next step: locate the leaking equipment (identify it by nameplate model and serial number), photograph the equipment nameplate and the area around the leak, and describe which seal and the leak rate — send the photos and I will provide the seal specification for that exact equipment.

Encoder on the axis is not sending signals. Position sensing is gone.
Evidence (work-order): axis/encoder identity not clear; tag is dirty/damaged and unreadable; two identical axis systems are running; no part number recorded.

I cannot recommend an encoder replacement without knowing which axis — per the provided work-order, your facility has two identical axis systems and the unreadable tag means the identity is not established. Replacing the encoder on the wrong axis masks the real fault. Safety floor: before any axis work, LOTO the motor and axis drive (axis faults can cause unexpected motion) — establish mechanical locks or breaks on the load to prevent drift — and never assume an axis is safe to work on even when power is off. Next step: go to the axis showing no encoder signal, clean the encoder nameplate so you can read it fully, take a photo of the readable nameplate and the axis drive nameplate, and describe which axis/joint it controls — send the photos and I will confirm the encoder model and replacement procedure for that exact system.

Solenoid won't open the valve. The coil might be bad or stuck.
Evidence (report): solenoid/valve not identified; similar solenoid-valve pairs on three production lines; no electrical test performed; no photo.

A solenoid that will not open could be electrically dead, mechanically stuck, or receiving no control signal — per the provided report, the identity is not established. Your facility has three similar solenoid-valve pairs; without identifying which one is not responding, I cannot tell you whether to test the coil resistance or inspect for mechanical blockage. Safety floor: before any solenoid work, LOTO the line (depressurize or isolate upstream flow) — do not force open a stuck solenoid (risk of stem shear or sudden flow release) — and use proper PPE for any high-pressure vent. Next step: go to the solenoid that is not responding, take a photo of its nameplate, describe which production line it controls, and test the coil with a multimeter if you have one — send the photo and your test result, and I will advise whether the fault is electrical or mechanical.

There's a grinding noise coming from somewhere on the assembly line. Might be a bad bearing.
Evidence (report): noise heard but source not located; similar bearing assemblies on two motor mounts; no vibration measurement taken; no photo or location detail.

A grinding noise could come from a bearing, gear, pulley, or brush contact — per the provided report, the location is not established. Your assembly line has similar bearings on two motor mounts and the noise source is not pinpointed. I cannot advise on bearing replacement when the identity is unclear. Safety floor: never locate a grinding noise by running the machine — LOTO the motor and use a listening device to isolate the sound without risk of contact — if the bearing is hot, use a non-contact thermometer and LOTO before any bearing work. Next step: use a stethoscope or sound-locating method to pinpoint which motor mount the noise is coming from, take a photo of that bearing's nameplate or the motor it supports, and note the temperature and noise characteristics — send the photo and description, and I will guide the bearing inspection and replacement for that exact location.

Oil temperature is climbing. Cooling is not keeping up. Should I lower the viscosity or change the filter?
Evidence (report): high oil temp observed; multiple hydraulic circuits in the facility; no temperature sensor identified; no system schematic or baseline temp available.

Oil temperature rise in a hydraulic system is a symptom — per the provided report, which system is hot is not established. I cannot recommend a change without identifying which system and why temperature is rising. Causes range from internal leakage, worn equipment, blocked cooler, or excessive load — each has a different remedy. Changing viscosity or filter on a system with a blocked cooler masks the real problem. Safety floor: do not disable a high-temperature alarm or override a thermostat to hide the symptom — elevated oil temperature degrades seals and accelerates wear — always LOTO before opening a system or touching a hot cooler. Next step: identify which hydraulic circuit is running hot, measure the current oil temperature and the desired baseline, check if the cooler intake is clear or blocked, and take a photo of the system nameplate and thermostat setting — send the photo and temperature info, and I will diagnose the cause for that system.

Equipment is vibrating. Something is out of balance or loose.
Evidence (work-order): vibration felt but not measured; multiple rotating components on the line; no handheld vibration meter data; no location marked.

Vibration can come from imbalance, misalignment, bearing wear, loose fasteners, or bent shafts — per the provided work-order, the location is not marked. Your equipment has many rotating components and without locating and measuring the vibration, the identity is not established. I cannot tell which one is failing. Safety floor: never investigate vibration by hand while the equipment is running — if vibration is severe, LOTO the equipment immediately and inspect visually for obvious loose parts or debris — use a handheld vibration meter or bearing thermometer if available, and never touch moving parts. Next step: visually inspect rotating shafts, couplings, and bearing housings for obvious damage, use a screwdriver handle to feel the vibration and narrow down the source, and if a handheld vibration meter is available, take readings and record the values — send a description or photos of the suspected component and any measurement data, and I will guide the balancing or repair for that source.

Saw an arc flash in one of the panels. Lights flickered. Could be a loose connection somewhere.
Evidence (report): arcing observed but source not identified; multiple panels and disconnects in the area; no circuit traced; no damage inspection performed.

An arc flash is an immediate electrical hazard and fire risk — per the provided report, the source is not identified. I cannot troubleshoot without confirming the source and stopping any energized work. Your facility has multiple panels; if arcing is still occurring, the source must be isolated and inspected by a qualified electrician. Safety floor: if you observed arcing, STOP all work immediately — do not attempt to locate or inspect the arc source yourself — arc flash hazard requires a qualified electrician with proper arc-flash PPE, no energized work near arcing. Call your electrical team immediately; do not re-energize until the fault is found and repaired. Next step: ensure the circuit that arced is still isolated, mark the area as hazardous, and notify your electrical team with the time, location, and any visible damage — do not proceed with production until the electrical fault is repaired and verified by qualified personnel.

Motor won't start. Breaker keeps tripping. How do I get it running?
Evidence (work-order): motor not identified; two motors on the line with similar breaker sizes; no electrical test performed; no fault current measured.

A motor that will not start with a tripping breaker points to a fault — per the provided work-order, which motor is not identified. I cannot diagnose without knowing which motor, its nameplate rating, and the trip current. Your facility has two similar motors and resetting the breaker blind risks motor damage or fire. Safety floor: do not keep resetting a tripping breaker to force the motor to start — a persistent trip means a fault exists — LOTO the motor circuit and call a qualified electrician to measure insulation resistance and rotor free-spin before any restart attempt. Next step: identify which motor is not starting (location, nameplate, horsepower, and any model/serial number), note the breaker size and trip count, and describe any sounds or smells from the motor — send this information, and I will guide a safe diagnostic sequence for that motor.

Compressor is cycling on and off a lot. Something is wrong with the pressure switches.
Evidence (report): cycling observed; two compressor units on site; no pressure readings recorded; no switch test performed; no nameplate checked.

A compressor cycling rapidly can indicate low cutoff pressure set too high, a leak, a bad check valve, or a stuck pressure switch — per the provided report, which compressor is not identified. I cannot advise when your facility has two compressor units and the identity is not established. Without identifying which one is cycling, I cannot tell you whether to adjust the cutoff or replace the switch. Safety floor: before any work on a compressor or pressure switch, LOTO the motor and depressurize the tank (open the drain valve fully) — do not assume pressure is gone just because the equipment stopped — and use proper PPE when relieving compressed air. Next step: identify which compressor is cycling rapidly (check nameplate model and serial), measure the current cutoff pressure, check for any obvious air leaks near fittings, and take a photo of the compressor nameplate and pressure-switch location — send the photo and pressure readings, and I will confirm the correct setpoint for that unit.

Filter pressure is running high. Probably clogged. Should I change it now or wait?
Evidence (report): high filter pressure observed; two identical filter housings on the system; no baseline pressure recorded; no flow rate measured; no filter age known.

High filter pressure can mean the filter is clogged, the differential-pressure switch is stuck, or the filter bypass has opened — per the provided report, which filter is not identified. I cannot advise on change timing when your facility has two identical housings and the identity is not established. If I assume the wrong one is high, the real clogged filter stays in service and eventually bypass opens. Safety floor: do not ignore a persistently high filter-pressure alarm — when bypass opens, the filter is effectively offline and contamination reaches downstream components — LOTO before opening any filter housing, and depressurize the bowl before loosening the band clamp. Next step: identify which filter assembly is reading high (location, manufacturer, model number, and any pressure gauge), record the current differential-pressure reading, note any visible dirt/discoloration on the visible element or bowl, and check the filter change date — send a photo of the nameplate and pressure gauge, and I will confirm the change interval and procedure for that filter.

Temperature control is not working. The setpoint is not staying where I set it.
Evidence (report): control not holding setpoint; multiple temperature zones in the facility; no baseline setpoint recorded; no sensor data logged.

A control not holding setpoint can be caused by a failed sensor, a stuck valve, a control-loop misconfiguration, or a dead control module — per the provided report, which temperature zone is not identified. I cannot advise a fix when your facility has multiple zones and the identity is not established. Without knowing which one is drifting, I cannot tell you whether to replace a sensor, recalibrate a setpoint, or inspect a valve. Safety floor: before any control work, confirm the system is stable — do not open a valve or change a setpoint while the system is in transient overshoot — LOTO before any sensor or valve replacement, and use proper PPE for high-temperature components or pressurized systems. Next step: identify which temperature zone is not holding setpoint (description: cooling circuit, oven, chiller, or room), note the setpoint you set and the actual temperature, and photograph the control or control panel serving that zone — send the photo and description, and I will diagnose the control fault for that zone.

Proximity switch is not detecting objects. Position sensing is gone.
Evidence (report): sensor not triggering; three identical sensors on the line; no sensor location marked; tag is missing; no electrical test performed.

A proximity switch that stops detecting can be contaminated, electrically disconnected, coil failed, or the target object is out of range — per the provided report, which sensor is not identified. I cannot troubleshoot when your facility has three identical sensors and the identity is not established. If I assume the wrong one, the real fault is left undetected. Safety floor: before any sensor work, LOTO the circuit powering the sensor — do not assume low voltage is safe; confirm with a meter — and do not force an obstruction into a sensor's field. Next step: locate the sensor that is not detecting, clean the sensor face (wipe away any dirt or oil), take a photo of the sensor nameplate and the wire connection, and describe the range and target — send the photo and description, and I will advise the proper test and fix for that sensor.

Got a capacitor failure in one of the motors. How do I replace it?
Evidence (report): capacitor fault suspected; two motors with capacitor-start circuits; no scope measurement or electrical test done; device not identified.

A failed run or start capacitor requires identifying which motor, the capacitor type, the voltage rating, and the microfarad value — per the provided report, which motor is not identified. I cannot provide a replacement part or procedure when your facility has two motors with capacitors and the identity is not established. Using the wrong capacitor risks catastrophic failure or electrical fire. Safety floor: before ANY capacitor work, LOTO the motor and allow minutes for discharge — then actively discharge the capacitor by shorting the terminals with an insulated screwdriver, no energized work near capacitors — never assume a capacitor is safe by looking at it. Next step: identify which motor has the capacitor fault (nameplate model and location), LOTO the motor, safely discharge the capacitor using the procedure above, photograph the capacitor nameplate (voltage rating, capacitance in microfarads, and type), and note any visible damage or bulging — send the photo and description, and I will confirm the replacement part number and procedure.

Input module is stuck high. The sensor should be sending a signal but it's not responding to the actual condition.
Evidence (report): input card not identified; multiple I/O modules in the cabinet; no scope trace available; sensor identity unclear.

A module input stuck high can be a dead sensor, a shorted wire, a bad card channel, or a disconnected input — per the provided report, which input module is not identified. I cannot troubleshoot when your cabinet has multiple I/O modules and the identity is not established. Without identifying the channel, I cannot tell you whether to check the sensor or test the card. Safety floor: before any I/O card work, LOTO the system power supply — do not assume system voltage is safe; confirm with a meter — and use a grounded wrist strap when handling or inserting cards, no energized work on open terminals. Next step: locate the stuck input in the software, trace that address to the physical I/O module and terminal number, take a photo of the I/O module nameplate and the specific terminal, and describe which sensor feeds that input — send the photo and description, and I will guide a safe diagnostic for that channel.

Transformer is overheating. Coolant temp is running high. What do I check?
Evidence (maintenance ticket): transformer not identified; two identical units in the substation; no temp sensor readings recorded; gauge unconfirmed.

I cannot troubleshoot a transformer without identifying which unit is overheating — per the provided maintenance ticket, your substation has two identical transformers and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate per maintenance-namespace-builder-spec, I must confirm: site / area / line / machine / asset / component context before troubleshooting. Without this, I cannot guide a safe inspection. Safety floor: never open a transformer housing without proper PPE — LOTO the supply, wait for cool-down, use grounded tools only, no energized work on transformers. Next step: locate the overheating transformer (check nameplate, serial, incoming line), photograph it with nameplate visible, measure actual coolant temperature, and describe which unit — send the photo and I will diagnose for that exact transformer.

Blower is making noise. Sounds like it's out of balance or damaged.
Evidence (work order): noise heard; three blower units in the facility; no vibration meter available; technician heard it from a distance.

I cannot guide a blower repair without locating which one is noisy — per the provided work order, your facility has three blower units and the noise source is not pinpointed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, the identity must be confirmed before troubleshooting. If I advise on the wrong unit, the real fault stays running. Safety floor: loud blower noise can indicate a thrown rotor blade — if so, blade breakage becomes a projectile hazard — LOTO the blower immediately and do NOT run it if noise is severe, no energized operation near damaged fans. Next step: go to each blower location, listen carefully to pinpoint which one is noisy, check for vibration or visible damage, take a photo of that blower's nameplate — send the location and photo, and I will guide service for that unit.

Controller is not communicating with the network. It looks like a connection issue.
Evidence (ticket): communication failure noted; two controllers on the system; no network diagnostics performed; cable connections not verified.

I cannot troubleshoot a communication failure without identifying which controller is offline — per the provided ticket, your system has two controllers and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, I need confirmed context before starting diagnosis. Acting on the wrong controller masks the real fault. Safety floor: before touching any network cable, ensure you are not introducing a single-point-of-failure — if the offline controller is critical to system safety, do not disconnect it further, LOTO before cable replacement, no energized work on critical controls. Next step: physically locate the controller showing no comms (check status lights, ping it from another device), verify its network cable is fully seated, and photograph the controller nameplate and Ethernet port — send the photo and describe which system it controls, and I will guide the network diagnostic for that controller.

Network switch is showing a port error. One port is not connecting.
Evidence (report): port failure observed; two managed switches in the system; no LED diagnostics recorded; port number not recorded.

I cannot guide a port troubleshooting without identifying which switch and which port — per the provided report, your system has two managed switches and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, confirmed asset identity is non-negotiable before troubleshooting. If I assume the wrong one, you troubleshoot the healthy device and leave the broken one offline. Safety floor: before replacing any cable or power-cycling a switch, confirm the device controls non-safety systems or has a backup path — power-cycling a network device can disrupt controls, LOTO before work, no energized disconnection of critical networks. Next step: locate the switch showing the error (check the status panel, LED indicators), identify the exact port number, check cable connections at both ends, and photograph the switch model and failing port's LED status — send the photo and port number, and I will advise the diagnostic steps.

Accumulator pressure is dropping. Losing power assist over the course of hours.
Evidence (maintenance log): pressure loss noted; two hydraulic accumulators in the system; no pressure gauge reading recorded; circuit identification missing.

I cannot diagnose pressure loss without identifying which accumulator and which circuit — per the provided maintenance log, your system has two accumulators and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, I need resolved technical context before troubleshooting. Pressure loss can have multiple causes. Safety floor: accumulators store pressure and can rupture if over-pressurized or if internal integrity fails — before any work, relieve pressure using isolation and bleed valves, then LOTO the pump, no energized work on pressurized accumulators, no working near rupture hazards. Next step: locate the accumulator showing pressure drop (measure current pressure, check isolation valve, listen for leaks), identify which hydraulic circuit it serves, and photograph the accumulator nameplate and pressure gauge reading — send the photo and pressure data, and I will guide the service steps.

Backup generator won't start. It's not responding to the control signal.
Evidence (work order): generator non-responsive; two generators on site; no unit identified; no manual available.

I cannot troubleshoot a non-starting generator without identifying which one and what type — per the provided work order, your site has two generators and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, I need resolved technical context before troubleshooting. A no-start fault can have multiple causes. Safety floor: before any generator work, confirm that fuel lines are isolated (LOTO the fuel pump), electrical power is removed (LOTO the battery or main), and the unit is cool — generators store heat and spinning components can be a hazard even after shutdown, no energized work near generators. Next step: locate the generator that won't start (check fuel tank level, battery voltage, any error codes on the control panel), photograph the generator's nameplate and control display, and describe the type (diesel, gas, propane), power rating, and the last successful start date — send the photo and details, and I will guide the start-sequence diagnostic.

Cable is damaged somewhere in the conduit run. Not sure where exactly.
Evidence (report): damage suspected; four cable runs between the same two enclosures; no insulation fault traced; no visual inspection done.

I cannot guide a cable repair without identifying which cable and where the damage is — per the provided report, your conduit has four runs and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, I must resolve which cable before troubleshooting. Repairing the wrong cable wastes time and leaves the real fault live. Safety floor: before any cable work, LOTO the power supply — a pinched or damaged cable can short and create a fault or arc flash hazard, no energized work on damaged cables — never assume a cable is de-energized without testing it with a meter. Next step: physically trace each cable from source to destination, look for visible damage or wet insulation, use a multimeter to measure insulation resistance on each cable against ground, and identify which cable is faulted — send a description of the location and cable identity, and I will advise whether to replace, splice, or repair.

Belt is slipping. Power is not being transmitted efficiently.
Evidence (observation): slip observed; two belt-driven machines on the line; no tension measurement taken; no speed comparison made.

I cannot troubleshoot belt slip without identifying which drive and which belt — per the provided observation, your line has two belt-driven machines and the identity is not confirmed. From the UNS location-confirmation gate, I need resolved technical context before troubleshooting. Slip can have multiple causes. Safety floor: before any belt tension work, LOTO the motor and confirm the pulley is not spinning — reaching near a rotating belt is a pinch hazard, no energized work on belt drives — use a belt tension gauge if available, and never rely on hand-feel alone. Next step: visually inspect both belt-driven machines for visible wear or contamination, measure the belt tension or deflection at the slack span, compare the motor speed to the output speed (if possible), and photograph the belt and pulley area showing the drive name or model — send the photo and your observations, and I will advise the belt service procedure.

Fan stopped running. One of them is definitely out.
Evidence (report): fan outage noted; three identical cooling fans; no unit location marked; no power check performed.
